title: It's Time to Embrace AI Literacy for Kids
author: Kiryn Hoffman, Erin Mote, and Lynne Parker
summary: Three leaders in children's museums, edtech, and technology policy argue that AI has become such a polarizing topic -- alternately treated as existential threat or transformational opportunity -- that adults are failing children by not building a shared, constructive vocabulary around it. Writing after a convening at the National Children's Museum, the authors say the real opportunity is not just teaching kids to use AI tools but teaching them how AI works, so critical thinking becomes the mechanism that lets children see both where AI augments human effort and where it 'fails miserably.' They frame this as urgent workforce and civic preparation, citing the World Economic Forum's projection that 39% of workers' core skills will change by 2030, and they explicitly ask adults to have the humility to admit they don't fully understand AI either, since even its own creators say generative AI has surpassed their understanding. The piece surveys early efforts -- Sesame Street/Google collaborations, Common Sense Media's grade-level AI literacy lessons, Children and Screens' research hub, hands-on museum exhibits -- as a starting toolkit, while arguing there needs to be far more investment in foundational AI understanding, not just tool-use training. Their closing argument is explicitly a course-correction from social media: society failed to have this conversation early enough with kids about platforms, and should not repeat that mistake with AI.
points: The authors' central reframe is teaching kids how AI works, not just how to use it -- arguing that understanding the mechanism (where it augments effort, where it fails) builds durable critical thinking rather than passive tool dependence.

They tie AI literacy directly to workforce preparation, citing the World Economic Forum's projection that 39% of workers' core skills will change by 2030 as a rationale for starting AI literacy young.

The piece explicitly frames AI literacy as a corrective to the social-media era: 'something we didn't do early enough' with kids and online platforms, and a mistake the authors argue society should not repeat with AI.

They call out a specific asymmetry adults must acknowledge -- most parents and educators 'didn't grow up with' AI and experts believe generative AI has already surpassed even its creators' full understanding -- as grounds for adults to learn alongside kids rather than pretend expertise.
quotes: About 62% of U.S. adults report interacting with AI several times a week, and adults and children alike engage on a regular basis with AI without even realizing it.

What if, alongside helping our youngest learn to use AI, we placed greater emphasis on teaching them how it works? By nurturing children’s critical thinking skills, we give them the power to understand it as a tool—where it can augment human effort, and where it fails miserably.
According to the World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report, employers expect that 39% of workers’ core skills will change by 2030, with technological skills gaining importance most rapidly.

As adults, we have the responsibility of fostering children’s safe use of this powerful tool. But let’s give ourselves the grace to acknowledge that we don’t understand AI either. We didn’t grow up with it, and experts and technology leaders believe that generative AI has surpassed the understanding of its creators.

By approaching this with curiosity, we can thoughtfully consider appropriate uses and guardrails for kids—something we didn’t do early enough when America’s children first began using online tools like social media.

AI’s purpose is not to replace human life, but to enhance it. Yet, the current conversation — especially around children’s use of AI — is too passive, treating these complex systems as inevitable rather than intentional creations.
